items.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So I learned a lot playing with his bands.

ctx.x: But it‟s all experience. That‟s about all until the end of school. I figure I ended school in 1950, I guess. I was writing a lot for rehearsal bands around. Sometimes I‟d take charts back to Westlake and have their band play it. I was playing the horn, going to sessions. I became friendly with Gene Roland, who was with the Kenton band – a lot of other bands. He was – he had a funny way of insinuating himself into a band. He was writing for Stan and traveling on the road with him. This was when Stan only had eight…

But he wrote hot. He was a jazz writer. So I learned a lot playing with his bands. Art Farmer played with one of his bands, I remember. Gene was at the house one night. As a joke – with his meat and potatoes orientation, he didn‟t want to know anything about twelve-tone music or Schoenberg – so, as a gag, I pulled out the recording of a chart I had made at Westlake which was a twelve-tone blues, which I guess every writer has to do at least once, just to prove you can do it. But I‟d made a big-band chart of this…

items.title: Bill Holman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: Gene Roland got me an interview with Stan on the strength of something I’d done in school

ctx.x: He certainly generates discussion about where he fits in jazz history. How do you feel about his place?

Well there’s a definite place there. I don’t know, not being a historian it would be hard to say where it fits but he did a lot of things, he gave opportunities to a whole lot of people that were able to go on their own and have good careers. A lot of his music, well I liked very much. Well the late 40s, the thing Rugulo was selling. I liked those a lot at the time. Then later in the 50s, when I was into it I liked more swinging things. So that’s why I wasn’t able to write for him for a while, because I didn’t…
It sounds like right up his alley.
